COMPLETE EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

────────────────────────────────────────  
1. Identification Strategy  
────────────────────────────────────────  
Strategy: Fuzzy Regression-Discontinuity Design (FRDD) around the EPA’s 1982 Hazard-Ranking-System (HRS) cutoff of 28.5, combined with a Difference-in-Differences (RDD-DiD) panel specification that subtracts pre-Superfund (1980 Census) outcomes from post-listing outcomes (1990, 2000).

Why appropriate  
• Assignment to the first National Priorities List (NPL) jumped sharply at 28.5, yet the score itself is continuous and was set after scoring.  
• Sites just above and below 28.5 are plausibly comparable on unobservables; the listing probability has a discontinuity ≈ 0.65–0.75, so FRDD is feasible.  
• Most welfare effects materialise years later; combining RD with DiD (i) purges any pre-existing level differences and (ii) improves precision in a sparse, 3-period panel.  

────────────────────────────────────────  
2. Treatment and Control  
────────────────────────────────────────  
Treatment Variable  
T_i = 1 if tract (or 2-mile circle) contains an HRS-tested site that scores above 28.5 in 1982.  
(For fuzzy RD, actual treatment is NPL_listing_i; T_i serves as instrument.)  

Control Group  
Sites with 1982 HRS scores just below 28.5 (e.g., 20 ≤ HRS < 28.5 using optimal bandwidth); their surrounding tracts/circles provide the counterfactual evolution absent federal cleanup.  

Treatment Timing  
“Event date” is 1983 initial NPL listing. Outcomes are measured in 1980 (pre), 1990 (medium-run), and 2000 (long-run). The estimating equation uses ΔY_1980-1990 and ΔY_1980-2000 as dependent variables.  

Running Variable & Cutoff  
R_i  = 1982 HRS composite score  
c    = 28.5  

────────────────────────────────────────  
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
────────────────────────────────────────  
A1. Continuity: Potential outcomes and covariates are smooth in HRS at 28.5.  
  Plausibility: Cutoff chosen ex-post for budgetary, not risk, reasons; no evidence EPA or firms could manipulate scores pre-announcement.  

A2. No Precise Manipulation: Density of HRS is continuous at 28.5.  
  Plausibility: Scores calculated by EPA from field data before cutoff set. Will formally test with McCrary.  

A3. First-Stage Relevance & Monotonicity: Probability of NPL listing rises at least weakly at cutoff and no sites drop in probability when crossing cutoff.  
  Plausibility: Historical records show ~90 % of > 28.5 sites listed, < 20 % of < 28.5 sites listed.  

A4. Stable Unit Treatment (SUTVA): Spillovers across sites within the estimation bandwidth do not differentially affect tracts on opposite sides of cutoff.  
  Plausibility: Geographic bandwidth (2-mile radius) keeps inter-site spillovers rare; will drop sites with overlapping buffers in robustness.  

A5. Parallel Trends (for DiD overlay): In absence of treatment, near-threshold tracts would have changed similarly after 1980.  
  Plausibility: Short geographic distances and RD local comparability support this; will verify pre-trends using 1970-1980 change.  

────────────────────────────────────────  
4. Main Threats & Mitigation  
────────────────────────────────────────  
Threat 1: Manipulation of HRS scores (gaming)  
  Check: McCrary density test; covariate balance; inspect digit-heaping.  
  Mitigation: If evidence of manipulation, narrow bandwidth, use donut RD excluding ±0.5 points around 28.5.  

Threat 2: Other policies correlate with HRS score (e.g., state cleanups or zoning).  
  Mitigation: Control for state-by-year FE; collect data on state remediation programs; include site-specific linear trends.  

Threat 3: Heterogeneous treatment timing (cleanups finish at different dates).  
  Mitigation: Instrument actual remediation progress (e.g., % of budget spent by 1990/2000) with listing; run event-time RD stacking each site-level year; show results robust to censoring sites without complete cleanup by 2000.  

────────────────────────────────────────  
5. R Code Outline (executable)  
────────────────────────────────────────  
```r
# 0. Packages --------------------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)      # fast high-dim FE & IV
library(rdrobust)    # RD inference
library(rddensity)   # McCrary test

# 1. Load Data -------------------------------------------------------------
tract   <- read_csv("tract_outcomes.csv")      # harmonised census data
sites   <- read_csv("superfund_sites.csv")     # HRS scores etc.
cross   <- read_csv("tract_site_crosswalk.csv")# which tract within 2-mile

# 2. Merge & Construct Analysis File --------------------------------------
df <- cross %>% 
      left_join(sites, by = "site_id") %>% 
      left_join(tract, by = c("tract_id","year"))

# Keep initial 1983 candidates only
df <- df %>% filter(initial_candidate == 1)

# 3. Variable Construction -------------------------------------------------
df <- df %>% 
  mutate(
    above28  = as.numeric(hrs_score >= 28.5),
    running  = hrs_score - 28.5,          # centered running var
    npl_list = as.numeric(npl_listing == 1),
    
    # Outcomes – changes wrt 1980
    d_price_90 = median_price[year==1990] - median_price[year==1980],
    d_price_00 = median_price[year==2000] - median_price[year==1980]
  )

# Collapse to one obs per site/tract --------------------------------------
analysis <- df %>% 
  group_by(site_id, tract_id) %>% 
  summarise(across(c(running, above28, npl_list,
                     d_price_90, d_price_00), first),
            .groups="drop")

# 4. Balance & McCrary -----------------------------------------------------
rddensity(analysis$running, analysis$above28)   # prints manipulation test
# Covariate example
feols(ln(household_income_1980) ~ above28 + running | 0,
      data = analysis %>% filter(abs(running) <= 10))

# 5. Main Fuzzy RD (2SLS within optimal bw) -------------------------------
bw <- rdbwselect(y = analysis$d_price_00,
                 x = analysis$running, c = 0)$bws[1] # Imbens–Kalyanaraman

est <- feols(d_price_00 ~ 1 |  (npl_list ~ above28),
             data = analysis %>% filter(abs(running) <= bw),
             vcov = "HC1")

summary(est)

# 6. Robustness: Polynomial & Bandwidth Sensitivity -----------------------
for(b in c(5,7.5,10)){
  tmp <- feols(d_price_00 ~ poly(running,2) | (npl_list ~ above28),
               data = analysis %>% filter(abs(running) <= b),
               vcov="HC1")
  cat("Bandwidth: ", b, "\n"); print(summary(tmp, cluster = ~site_id))
}

# 7. Placebo Cutoff --------------------------------------------------------
placebo <- analysis %>% 
           mutate(above25 = as.numeric(running >= -3.5 & running < -0.0))

feols(d_price_00 ~ above25 + running | 0,
      data = placebo %>% filter(abs(running + 3.5) <= bw),
      vcov = "HC1")
```

────────────────────────────────────────  
6. Expected Results (Priors)  
────────────────────────────────────────  
Direction: Positive. Cleaning a serious hazardous site should raise housing prices/rents and possibly attract higher-income residents; supply may expand modestly (new construction).  

Magnitude (very rough):  
• Median house prices within 2 miles: +4 % to +8 % by 2000 (≈ $6k–$12k on a $150k base).  
• Rental rates: +3 %–5 %.  
• Population: small net inflow (1-2 %).  
Implication: Capitalised benefits per site of $20–40 million, within the ballpark of mean remediation costs, suggesting benefits may roughly offset costs.  

────────────────────────────────────────  
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RDD)  
(1 = clearly satisfied; 0 = questionable)  

C1: Density of running variable smooth at cutoff        → 1  
C2: Baseline covariates smooth at cutoff                → 1  
C3: Large, monotone first-stage discontinuity           → 1  
C4: No other policy discontinuity at 28.5               → 0.5 (state cleanups?)  
C5: Robust to bandwidth & polynomial choice             → 1  

Total = 4.5 / 5.
